modules.title: Caregiver involvement and family support
modules.outcome: Plan bounded caregiver engagement that considers the young person's views, safety and evidence limits.

teaching_points.text: Caregiver involvement needs context-specific consideration.
Practical family support differs from clinical family intervention.
The parenting review has population and delivery limits.
Missed sessions can reflect access constraints.
Proposed help does not authorise all information sharing.

modules.title: School community pathways and transitions
modules.outcome: Specify a feasible intersectoral support pathway with qualified ownership and an appropriate review question.

teaching_points.text: A network map needs specific accepted roles.
A referral sent does not establish continuity.
International service examples do not prove local availability.
Readiness includes staff and access resources.
An access review is not a clinical recovery claim.

questions.question: A fictional adolescent misses a club after its timetable changes. What should a learner do first within this exercise?

options.text: Diagnose a disorder from absence alone.
Assume all non-attendance has one clinical cause.
Separate the observation from possible context and appropriate support questions.
Label the family responsible without further information.

questions.rationale: The observation needs contextual interpretation rather than an unsupported diagnosis.

questions.question: A support service uses identical explanations for every age and communication need. What should be reviewed?

options.text: Only whether the form has a logo.
A rule that all ages understand options identically.
A requirement that children disclose distress publicly.
Whether explanations and participation opportunities fit the young person's development and access needs.

questions.rationale: Developmentally appropriate support includes accessible communication.

questions.question: A fictional caregiver's account differs from the adolescent's stated concern. What should a support outline avoid?

options.text: Automatically treating one account as the complete perspective without qualified consideration.
Retaining the difference as information to consider.
Using appropriate safeguarding procedures.
Identifying communication needs.

questions.rationale: Different accounts should remain visible within a suitable qualified process.

questions.question: A fictional young person agrees to discuss an activity. What should not be assumed?

options.text: That an accessible explanation can help.
Permission for every disclosure, referral or legal decision.
That the young person's views matter.
That qualified local procedures remain necessary.

questions.rationale: Consent, assent and information permissions require decision-specific handling.

questions.question: A facilitator wants learners to interview children about distress as an assessment task. What fits this course instead?

options.text: Use the youngest available child as practice.
Collect identifying school and health records.
Analyse the supplied fictional descriptions without real interviews or screening.
Administer an unapproved clinical scale for marks.

questions.rationale: Introductory learning does not authorise real child assessment or sensitive collection.

questions.question: A fictional service assumes any accompanying adult may receive a child's full account. What needs review?

options.text: Only whether the adult arrived first.
A rule that accompaniment grants all authority.
A belief that privacy does not apply to young people.
The adult's role, safety, relevant permissions and qualified safeguarding process.

questions.rationale: Presence alone does not determine safe or authorised involvement.

questions.question: A caregiver helps organise transport to an appointment. What should not be inferred?

options.text: That the caregiver has delivered or is qualified to deliver family therapy.
That transport can affect access.
That role clarity is useful.
That the young person's priorities remain relevant.

questions.rationale: Different activities have different purposes and competency requirements.

questions.question: A learner applies the 2026 review to prove a mandated digital-only programme for all young children works. What is the problem?

options.text: A recent issue date validates every population.
The review concerns voluntary adolescent-parent programmes with face-to-face components and cannot justify that transfer.
Every parenting programme is the same intervention.
Narrative synthesis removes all applicability limits.

questions.rationale: Age, voluntary participation and delivery format constrain interpretation.

questions.question: A fictional caregiver misses a meeting that conflicts with paid work. What should be considered?

options.text: Proof that the caregiver does not care.
A diagnosis from the attendance record.
The timing barrier and feasible engagement options rather than an automatic motivation judgement.
A requirement to disclose more private information as a penalty.

questions.rationale: Attendance is affected by practical conditions as well as preferences.

questions.question: A school contact may help with access and requests the entire health history. What should a plan clarify?

options.text: Automatic full disclosure to anyone offering help.
A copy in the class worksheet.
A rule that intersectoral support cancels privacy.
The specific purpose, necessary information and appropriate permissions/qualified authority.

questions.rationale: Support coordination still requires proportionate authorised information handling.

questions.question: A fictional pathway lists many agencies but no one owns the next step. What should be added?

options.text: The relevant need, responsible role and accepted action between services.
More agency logos without responsibilities.
A promise that every listed agency has capacity.
An assumption that a diagram itself delivers care.

questions.rationale: Coordination requires clear actions and responsibility rather than a service list.

questions.question: An adolescent's transfer is marked complete before receiving-service acceptance. What is still unresolved?

options.text: Only whether the email was formatted well.
Eligibility, accepted responsibility and a feasible next contact within appropriate arrangements.
A guaranteed clinical outcome.
A rule that no one remains responsible after sending.

questions.rationale: Administrative transmission is not completed access or continuity.

questions.question: A learner promises a local specialist place because WHO describes an example elsewhere. What correction is needed?

options.text: Use the example's waiting time as a universal guarantee.
Assume all systems have identical eligibility.
Verify actual local scope and capacity through authorised roles before making an availability claim.
Treat a source citation as a booking confirmation.

questions.rationale: Examples inform comparison rather than establish current local service status.

questions.question: A fictional pathway has agreed arrows but no trained staff or access arrangements. How should it be described?

options.text: Ready solely because the map is complete.
Approved because the title includes psychosocial support.
A substitute for independent safeguarding review.
Conditional on resolving the staffing and access dependencies.

questions.rationale: Implementation needs conditions beyond an administrative design.

questions.question: A fictional handover review confirms the next appointment was accessible. What remains a separate question?

options.text: Clinical outcomes and any causal programme-effect claim.
Whether the referral action was documented.
Whether access was the stated review question.
Whether a responsible review role was named.

questions.rationale: Evidence of access supports a limited claim, not all health outcomes.

courses.title: Mental Health Service Coordination and Safe Referral
courses.cover_title:
Mental Health Service
Coordination and
Safe Referral
courses.school_name: School of Mental Health and Psychosocial Care
courses.audience: Introductory social work and community-service learners using fictional scenarios. No diagnosis, therapy, prescribing, crisis-triage authority or independent child/clinical practice is conferred. Qualified roles, local procedures and supervised skills remain necessary.
courses.study_guidance: Use only the supplied non-graphic fictional scenarios and invented aggregate data. Do not seek personal trauma histories, interview children or submit real health/service records. Write reasoning before checking feedback. You may pause or use an alternative fictional exercise. Supervised skills observation is separate.
courses.practice_safety_note: Use only the supplied non-graphic fictional scenario or invented aggregate data. Do not collect personal trauma histories, interview children or submit real health records. You may pause or use an alternative fictional exercise. Record reasoning before checking guide feedback.
courses.outcome: Prepare a fictional mental-health support pathway with verified service fit, specific information permissions, accepted handover responsibility and a bounded continuity review within professional scope.

modules.title: Needs roles and service fit
modules.outcome: Distinguish non-clinical navigation from treatment coordination and specify a service-verification task.
paragraphs: Coordination helps connect a person's needs and preferences with suitable roles across services. It is more than giving someone a long list of contacts. Begin with the person's goal, the barrier to using support and the action each service can actually take. The WHO community guidance links mental-health services with social supports and ordinary community life. An introductory worker may help clarify access questions within their role; making a diagnosis, changing medication, deciding clinical triage or directing treatment requires qualified authority. Do not infer that all activities described as coordination have the same competency requirements. [S21, S1]

The 2025 scoping review distinguishes varied clinical and non-clinical tasks described in adult mental-health coordination. Its included settings and eligibility rules differ considerably, and exclusion of case-management terminology may have missed similar models. The review maps concepts and reported experiences rather than proving one effective model for every service. Its examples are not a universal eligibility standard or a substitute for local role definitions. For a fictional plan, state which task is practical navigation, which requires qualified clinical judgement and which belongs to an organisational decision-maker. [R32, S21]

A service option needs current verification of scope, eligibility, cost, access, communication and capacity through authorised arrangements. A familiar name or an old directory entry does not establish that a person can use the service now. Consider whether transport, language, disability access, digital exclusion or scheduling affects fit. Do not promise acceptance, a waiting time or a particular outcome before appropriate confirmation. The 2025 policy introduction makes workforce and system conditions relevant to quality; shortages should be represented as a service dependency rather than silently treated as the person's responsibility. [S22, S21, S1]

In this exercise, use fictional services and identify what would need verification before an actual referral. Keep a directory-quality question separate from a clinical assessment and do not contact real patients, impersonate a professional or send a real health account as a test. Write the information status clearly: a proposed option, verified service information and acceptance for a particular person are different. A useful outline names the authorised role that will check the gap and the next appropriate decision if the option is unsuitable. A completed worksheet does not qualify an independent care coordinator. [S1, R32, S21]
modules.example: Fictional case: an adult needs an accessible appointment and transport support. A worker provides an old service list and marks care coordinated. The learner identifies the actual goal, verification questions and separate clinical and practical responsibilities.
modules.activity: Prepare a service-fit note with the person's goal, a practical barrier, service-status questions, clinical/non-clinical role distinction, verification owner and a conditional next step.
modules.feedback: A sound note identifies fit and authority rather than equating a directory with access. It retains uncertainty about current capacity and keeps treatment decisions with qualified roles.

modules.title: Permission handover and accepted responsibility
modules.outcome: Specify a bounded handover with suitable information and confirmed responsibility.
paragraphs: A referral should have a clear purpose that the person understands through appropriate communication. Permission to discuss options is not automatically permission to send a full record. Identify the minimum information needed for the specific receiving role, the relevant authority or consent arrangements and an approved channel. Do not promise confidentiality without limits or decide a real reporting exception from a classroom scenario. Clinical, safeguarding and local legal requirements may need qualified handling. A fictional handover note can name these questions without containing a real person's history or identifiers. [S1, S21]

Accepted responsibility matters at each stage. Clarify who sends the referral, who receives it, what confirmation is needed and who remains responsible while acceptance or access is unresolved. A message sent, a message received, a service accepted and assistance accessed are distinct statuses. The adult coordination review reports confusion, service gaps and workload barriers across settings, so a neat diagram cannot establish continuity. Agree a feasible next contact within authorised arrangements and explain limitations rather than assume silence means consent, attendance or a successful outcome. [R32, S21]

Routine referrals and urgent clinical or safeguarding concerns require different response arrangements. A worker should know the designated qualified route for the actual setting and use it when appropriate, rather than invent thresholds, assign a universal risk score or wait for a routine form to be processed. This course does not teach clinical triage, emergency treatment or physical intervention. The fictional exercise tests whether the learner recognises a scope boundary and responsible escalation dependency. It never asks learners to simulate a real crisis with an unprepared person or practise on someone in distress. [S21, S1]

Digital and peer options can be part of a support network, but they require appropriate scope, access, privacy, moderation and response arrangements. The 2026 digital peer-support review cannot validate an arbitrary group or guarantee that it will manage urgent needs. A person should be able to consider suitable alternatives without losing unrelated support. Record only necessary handover status in authorised systems, with realistic follow-up responsibility. If acceptance fails or preferences change, revisit options through the person and qualified roles; do not forward the same sensitive account more widely as an improvised solution. [R30, S21, S1]
modules.example: Fictional case: a worker sends a complete private account to several services and records a successful referral despite no acceptance. The adult had agreed only to discuss one option. The learner identifies the permission, minimum-information and responsibility gaps.
modules.activity: Draft a conditional handover outline with purpose, permission/authority check, necessary information, approved channel, sending/receiving responsibility, unresolved status and a qualified urgent-response boundary.
modules.feedback: A defensible outline separates discussion from permission to share and sending from acceptance. It assigns responsibility for gaps, preserves information boundaries and recognises qualified urgent procedures.

modules.title: Transitions measurement and service improvement
modules.outcome: Review access and continuity with defined measures and accountable action.
paragraphs: Transitions between services can expose gaps in responsibility, communication or access. A person may change location, age eligibility or support preferences while a referral is pending. A useful review asks what the next service has accepted, what the person understands and who will respond if the planned contact fails. The WHO policy introduction connects these questions with staffing, governance and resources. Do not turn a transition failure into an assumption of non-compliance, or record support as completed because a form moved successfully between two systems. [S22, S21, S1]

Measure the question you actually need to answer. In an invented exercise, nine of twelve eligible handovers achieve a defined first contact in one period, compared with twelve of twenty in another. These are seventy-five percent and sixty percent: the count increases while the proportion falls by fifteen percentage points. Comparability still depends on the definition, eligible group, period and missing information. These fictional aggregates do not measure population mental-health prevalence, clinical recovery or staff competence. Unknown contact status should remain unknown under an explicit rule rather than automatically be recorded as success. [R32, S21]

The coordination scoping review identifies reported barriers and varied models but calls for rigorous effectiveness research. The digital peer-support review also has limited long-term and safety reporting. Neither permits a programme to infer recovery, universal safety or causal benefit from a contact count. An appropriate service review needs a relevant outcome, defined source, coverage, ethical governance and a design suited to its claim. Do not copy a clinical questionnaire or collect actual health records for this worksheet; critique the invented data and proposed process instead. [R32, R30, S1]

A review should support a feasible response. Identify the barrier, the role authorised to act, a resource or service dependency, an agreed feedback route and a point to revisit the change. Preserve uncertainty and differing perspectives, including those who could not use the proposed pathway. Where the solution needs a clinical, safeguarding, legal or organisational decision, state that dependency clearly. The course develops introductory coordination reasoning, not authority to approve a service or independently manage treatment. All changes to actual practice require appropriate qualified review, and observed skills remain a separate requirement for professional responsibilities. [S22, S21, S1]
modules.example: Fictional dataset: nine of twelve eligible handovers achieve first contact in period A; twelve of twenty do so in B. A report calls the larger second count an improved rate and proof of recovery. The learner corrects the arithmetic and separates contact from clinical outcomes.
modules.activity: Calculate both proportions and the percentage-point change. Add definition/coverage checks, an unknown-status rule, an unsupported claim to remove and an accountable improvement owner.
modules.feedback: A is 75% and B is 60%, a decrease of 15 percentage points despite the higher count. First contact is a defined access observation, not demonstrated recovery or a causal programme effect.

assessment.title: Mental Health Service Coordination and Safe Referral

modules.title: Needs roles and service fit
modules.outcome: Distinguish non-clinical navigation from treatment coordination and specify a service-verification task.

teaching_points.text: Coordination begins with a person's goal and access needs.
Navigation and treatment coordination have different authority requirements.
An old directory does not verify current service fit.
A scoping review is not a universal eligibility standard.
A proposed option differs from person-specific acceptance.

modules.title: Permission handover and accepted responsibility
modules.outcome: Specify a bounded handover with suitable information and confirmed responsibility.

teaching_points.text: Discussing an option is not blanket consent to share records.
Sending and acceptance are different handover statuses.
Urgent concerns need the designated qualified response route.
A peer group is not automatically a crisis service.
Failed acceptance does not authorise wider disclosure.

modules.title: Transitions measurement and service improvement
modules.outcome: Review access and continuity with defined measures and accountable action.

teaching_points.text: Transition responsibility must remain explicit.
Counts and handover proportions can differ.
The percentage-point difference uses the two proportions.
First contact is not demonstrated clinical recovery.
A review finding needs a feasible accountable response.

questions.question: A fictional worker sends a long contact list without considering an adult's access barrier. What should be clarified?

options.text: Only the length of the directory.
A claim that every listed service is appropriate.
The goal, practical barrier and suitable role for the next action.
The worker's preferred diagnosis from the list.

questions.rationale: Useful coordination connects needs and feasible actions rather than merely supplying contacts.

questions.question: A support worker can arrange transport but is asked to alter medication. What boundary applies?

options.text: Any coordination task grants prescribing authority.
Transport planning is itself a medical prescription.
The course badge replaces clinical authorisation.
Medication decisions require an appropriately qualified clinical role.

questions.rationale: Practical assistance does not confer treatment competence.

questions.question: A fictional referral option comes from a years-old leaflet. What should be checked through authorised arrangements?

options.text: Current scope, eligibility, access, cost and capacity relevant to the person's needs.
Only the colour of its logo.
A universal acceptance guarantee from its name.
A real health history sent as a test.

questions.rationale: Service information can change and needs appropriate verification.

questions.question: A learner applies one reviewed service's entry criteria to every mental-health service. What is missing?

options.text: Permission to use any criterion because it was published.
Actual local service rules and context-specific verification.
Proof that all reviewed settings were identical.
A rule that no professional role differences exist.

questions.rationale: Examples from varied settings cannot establish universal criteria.

questions.question: A service's general information is current but it has not accepted a fictional referral. What is the accurate status?

options.text: Completed care and guaranteed recovery.
A confirmed booking solely from the directory.
A potentially suitable verified option with person-specific acceptance still unresolved.
Proof that no follow-up is needed.

questions.rationale: Information verification and an accepted referral are separate steps.

questions.question: A fictional adult agrees to hear about a service, but a worker sends the full record. What should have been clarified?

options.text: Only whether the file was large enough.
An assumption that all helpful uses are authorised.
A public copy so other learners can check it.
The specific referral purpose, appropriate permission/authority and necessary information.

questions.rationale: Information sharing needs its own appropriate basis and proportionate scope.

questions.question: A fictional referral email is sent but no service confirms acceptance. What remains necessary?

options.text: An assigned follow-up and clarity about responsibility while access is unresolved.
Automatic completion of care.
A conclusion that the adult attended.
A rule that no sender has further duties after pressing send.

questions.rationale: Continuity needs accepted actions and follow-up rather than transmission alone.

questions.question: A fictional support outline says all urgent concerns should wait for routine referral processing. What needs correction?

options.text: Invent one numerical threshold for every situation.
Use the setting's authorised qualified urgent clinical/safeguarding arrangements when applicable.
Let an introductory quiz score authorise clinical triage.
Practise an unprepared real crisis scenario.

questions.rationale: Routine administration must not substitute for appropriate urgent procedures.

questions.question: An unverified online peer forum is listed as the sole response to urgent clinical needs. What is missing?

options.text: A popularity score sufficient to guarantee safety.
An assumption that all peers are clinicians.
Verified appropriate scope and qualified response arrangements with suitable alternatives.
A universal promise based on the review's title.

questions.rationale: Digital peer support has different roles and evidence limits from urgent clinical care.

questions.question: One fictional service cannot accept a referral. What should a worker avoid?

options.text: Revisiting suitable options with the person.
Recording the unresolved status appropriately.
Seeking qualified advice within authorised arrangements.
Forwarding the full account to many others without appropriate purpose and permission.

questions.rationale: A service gap does not remove information-sharing boundaries.

questions.question: A fictional adult changes service eligibility while a referral is pending. What should be reviewed?

options.text: Accepted roles, suitable options and responsibility for the next contact or unresolved gap.
A rule that all responsibility ends at an age boundary.
An assumption that another service automatically accepted.
A diagnosis of non-compliance from the administrative change.

questions.rationale: Continuity depends on actual arrangements during changing circumstances.

questions.question: An invented service records nine of twelve first contacts, then twelve of twenty. What are the proportions?

options.text: Sixty percent followed by seventy-five percent.
Seventy-five percent followed by sixty percent.
Nine percent followed by twelve percent.
Both are twelve percent because contacts are counted.

questions.question: A fictional first-contact proportion changes from 75% to 60%. What is the absolute change?

options.text: An increase of fifteen percentage points.
No change because the contact count increased.
A decrease of fifteen percentage points.
A decrease of fifteen percent relative to 75%.

questions.rationale: The absolute difference is 60 minus 75 percentage points; relative change is different.

questions.question: A fictional report calls an achieved first contact proof that mental-health difficulties resolved. What is justified?

options.text: A clinical cure from the appointment record alone.
A causal effect established by counting contacts.
A validated prevalence estimate for the whole community.
A limited access observation, with clinical outcomes requiring separate appropriate evidence.

questions.rationale: The measure supports its defined contact status rather than broader health claims.

questions.question: A fictional continuity review identifies a recurring unaccepted handover. What should a recommendation specify?

options.text: An authorised owner, corrective action, dependency, feedback route and review point.
A success claim because more forms were sent.
Unrestricted linkage of all health records.
A promise that one worker can resolve every system gap.

questions.rationale: Service improvement connects a supported finding with authority, resources and follow-through.

evidence_note: Checked 15 November 2026. Current OA studies complement WHO/UNICEF service guidance and Nigerian IJSDS context. Publication and evidence dates differ. Actual file-page counts, reporting inconsistencies, restricted retrievals and rights are explicit. Q1/Q2 statements use SCImago's own indexed records for Trauma Violence and Abuse/Journal of Child and Family Studies; direct tables restricted, no independent JCR claim. Rank is not article validity. Clinical/safeguarding, Nigerian practice/legal, lived-experience, accessibility/pilot and supervised-skills reviews remain pending.
